etymology: A clipped, playful form of adorable, built on the same pattern as totes (totally), obvi (obviously), and amazeballs. It appears online in the late 2000s and peaked about 2012–2014; Oxford Dictionaries Online added it in 2014, to widespread grumbling. Used for babies, puppies, couples, outfits, and anything small and sweet, often in a deliberately baby-talk register.
biblical_def: Adorbs is adorable in baby-talk: "That puppy is adorbs." It is a harmless, affectionate word, mostly used by young women about small, sweet things. The Christian observation is less a correction than a curiosity, because the root word has travelled a long way down. In Webster’s 1828 dictionary, adorable meant first "That ought to be adored; worthy of divine honors," and only "in popular use" something worthy of great love. The word for what only God deserves became the word for a kitten in a teacup. Scripture reserves adoration for God: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker" (Psa 95:6). When John fell at an angel’s feet, he was stopped: "See thou do it not … worship God" (Rev 19:10). None of this means a Christian cannot call a baby adorable; delight in small, lovely things is a gift, and the Lord Himself took little children in His arms and blessed them (Mar 10:16). It does mean that a careful Christian notices what our words have lost. A father can let his daughter say "adorbs" about the puppy and also teach her the old meaning, so that when she sings "O come, let us adore Him" at Christmas she knows what the word was made for. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above" (Jas 1:17), including the puppy.
webster_summary: Millennial clipped slang (late 2000s; Oxford online 2014) for adorable, cute; harmless, though its root once meant "worthy of divine honors," a reminder that adoration belongs to God (Psa 95:6).
webster_full: ADORBS, adj. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s; clipped from adorable) Cute, sweet, charming. "Those tiny shoes are adorbs." Same pattern: totes, obvi, amazeballs.
Webster (1828), root adorable: ADORABLE, adjective That ought to be adored; worthy of divine honors. In popular use, worthy of the utmost love or respect.
Decode for parents: harmless; a teaching moment for what "adore" first meant.
scriptures: Psa 95:6
O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker.

And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches.
corruption_summary: Adorbs is harmless affection; its only lesson is the drift of its root, from "worthy of divine honors" to "cute," which reminds us to keep adoration for God.
corruption_paragraphs: If there is a corruption here, it belongs to the root, not the slang. Adorable fell from a word of worship to a word for cuteness long before Millennials clipped it. The drift is typical of a culture that spends its highest words on its smallest pleasures, so that language for God has to compete with language for brunch. Children who never hear the old meaning will not miss it, and they will sing "adore" in carols without feeling its weight.

The redemption is twofold. Enjoy the small sweet things, because they are God’s gifts: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all" (Psa 104:24). And keep a vocabulary of worship strong enough for worship. Teach the young to delight in puppies and babies, and to bow their knees to the only One who is truly adorable in the 1828 sense.
roots_summary: Latin adorare (to speak to, to worship) → adorable (worthy of divine honors; popularly, lovable) → late-2000s clipped adorbs → Oxford online 2014.
roots_lines: Latin ad + orare — to speak to, to pray to; adorare — to worship
17th c.: adorable — worthy of divine honors; later, popularly, delightful
Late 2000s: clipped adorbs, with totes, obvi
2014: added to Oxford Dictionaries Online
Biblical anchor: O come, let us worship and bow down (Psa 95:6); worship God (Rev 19:10)
usage: "Her baby in the little bear hat is adorbs."
Every good gift is from above (Jas 1:17), the puppy included.
Adore in the old sense only One: let us kneel before the LORD our maker (Psa 95:6).

etymology: A clipped form of obviously, from late-2000s Millennial speech and texting, part of the same family as totes, adorbs, probs (probably), and whatevs. It was popularized by teen television and comedy around 2010–2013 and often delivered with a self-aware, mock-valley-girl tone. Used to mark something as too plain to need explaining ("Are you coming?" "Obvi.").
biblical_def: Obvi means "obviously": of course, no need to ask. It is a small, breezy word, usually affectionate, sometimes condescending ("obvi you didn’t read it"). The Christian observation: the slang is harmless, and it raises a real question: what is obvious? Scripture says some truths are so plain that refusing them is without excuse. "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse" (Rom 1:20). "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psa 19:1). The existence of the Creator is, in the Bible’s view, obvi. Yet Scripture also says the obvious can be hidden from the proud: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Mat 11:25). What is plain to a humble child can be invisible to a clever adult who does not want to see. And Christians must take care not to use "obviously" as a weapon. The wise teacher remembers that what is obvious to him was once unknown, and answers questions "with meekness and fear" (1Pe 3:15). A father uses the word with his children as a little catechism: Does God see you? Obvi. Did Jesus rise? Obvi. And he teaches them to explain the obvious kindly to those who do not yet see it.
webster_summary: Millennial clipped slang (late 2000s) for obviously; harmless, and a reminder that Scripture calls God’s existence plain from creation (Rom 1:20) while asking us to explain the obvious with meekness (1Pe 3:15).
webster_full: OBVI, adv. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s; clipped from obviously) Obviously; of course. "Obvi I’m coming." Same family: totes, probs, whatevs.

Webster (1828), root obvious: OBVIOUS, adjective [Latin obvus. See the Verb.] 1. Meeting; opposed in front. I to the evil turn my obvious breast. [Not now used.] 2. Open; exposed. [ Little Used .] 3. Plain; evident; easily discovered, seen or understood; readily perceived by the eye or the intellect. We say, a phenomenon obvious to the sight, or a truth obvious to the mind.
Decode for parents: harmless; watch only for the condescending "obvi" toward slower siblings.
scriptures: Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Psa 19:1
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Pro 8:9
They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge.
corruption_summary: Obvi is harmless; its only shadow is condescension, while its root raises the question of what is truly obvious: the Creator, plain in His works.
corruption_paragraphs: The slight corruption in "obvi" is the eye-roll it can carry: the impatience of the person who knows toward the person who does not. Online culture rewards that tone, and it can leak into how Christians talk about their faith, as if every unbeliever were stupid rather than blind. Scripture’s plainness is real, but it never licenses contempt; the apostles reasoned, persuaded, and pleaded.

The redemption is to treat God’s plain truths as gifts to be shared. Wisdom says of her words, "They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge" (Pro 8:9). Teach children the obvious things early and firmly, so that the existence of God, the goodness of His law, and the reality of Christ’s resurrection are as plain to them as the sky; and teach them to explain those things gently to friends for whom they are not yet obvious.
roots_summary: Latin obviam (in the way, meeting) → obvius → English obvious (plain to see) → late-2000s clipped obvi.
roots_lines: Latin ob viam — in the way; obvius — meeting, at hand
17th c.: obvious — plain, evident
Late 2000s: Millennial clipped obvi, totes, probs
2010s: teen TV and comedy spread the tone
Biblical anchor: clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made (Rom 1:20)
usage: "Pizza night?" "Obvi."
The heavens declare the glory of God (Psa 19:1): the original obvi.
Explain the obvious with meekness and fear (1Pe 3:15).

etymology: A clipped form of crazy, doubled as cray-cray. It was used in hip-hop and online from the late 2000s and was made famous by a 2011 Jay-Z and Kanye West track whose refrain used it (in a line too coarse to quote); by 2012 it was general Millennial slang, often with a playful, mock-dramatic tone ("this week has been cray"). Merriam-Webster and others noted it by the mid-2010s.
biblical_def: Cray (or cray-cray) is crazy made cute: wild, chaotic, unbelievable, or impressively over the top. "The party was cray." "My aunt is cray-cray." The Christian observation: the slang itself is light, but it rides on a word that once named real suffering, and it praises a kind of wildness Scripture does not. The 1828 root meant broken, decrepit, "deranged; weakened or disordered in intellect." Scripture treats real madness with compassion and with hope: the man in the tombs among the Gadarenes was found, after Jesus came, "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mar 5:15). The playful use can be harmless, but casual mockery of the mentally ill is not, and the word slides easily into it ("she’s cray" about a girl in genuine distress). The second issue is the admiration of chaos. "Cray" is often praise: the night that got out of hand, the stunt that nearly killed someone. Scripture prizes the opposite, a sound mind: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). Paul, accused of madness by Festus, answered, "I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness" (Act 26:25). A father teaches his children to laugh at real absurdity, to be gentle with those whose minds are truly troubled, and to aim for the sound mind God gives, not the wildness the culture applauds.
webster_summary: Millennial clipped slang (late 2000s; 2011 hip-hop hit) for crazy: wild, chaotic, unbelievable; light in itself, but it can mock real affliction and praise chaos over the sound mind (2Ti 1:7).
webster_full: CRAY, adj. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s; clipped from crazy; also cray-cray) Crazy; wild; chaotic; unbelievable. "This week is cray."

Webster (1828), root crazy: CRAZY, adjective 1. Broken; decrepit; weak; feeble; applied to the body, or constitution, or any structure; as a crazy body; a crazy constitution; a crazy ship. 2. Broken, weakened, or disordered in intellect; deranged, weakened, or shattered in mind. We say, the man is crazy
Decode for parents: teach the difference between laughing at absurdity and mocking someone who is truly struggling.
scriptures: Mar 5:15
And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
Rom 12:3

For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
corruption_summary: Cray makes crazy cute; harmless as a joke, it can mock real affliction and praise chaos, while Scripture prizes the sound mind and restores the troubled.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption has two edges. One is cruelty by vocabulary: "cray" said of a classmate who is anxious, depressed, or genuinely ill turns suffering into a joke. The other is the celebration of the out-of-control: a culture that calls wild behaviour "cray" as praise is rewarding the loss of self-government. "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28).

The recovery is the sound mind and the healing touch. Paul asks believers "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly" (Rom 12:3). Sobriety of mind is not dullness; it is clarity, the ability to see things as they are. Teach the young to keep their humour kind, to pray for and befriend the troubled rather than label them, and to remember that the Lord Jesus sought out the man the town called mad and sent him home in his right mind.
roots_summary: Old Norse krasa (to shatter) → craze → crazy (cracked, broken; then deranged) → late-2000s clipped cray, cray-cray.
roots_lines: Old Norse krasa — to shatter; Middle English crasen — to break
16th c.: crazy — cracked, frail; 17th c.: unsound of mind
Late 2000s: hip-hop and online cray; 2011 hit popularizes it
2012–: general Millennial slang; cray-cray
Biblical anchor: sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind (Mar 5:15); a sound mind (2Ti 1:7)
usage: "Twelve kids at one sleepover? That’s cray."
God hath given us a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).
Jesus sent the man the town called mad home in his right mind (Mar 5:15).

etymology: A jokey intensification of amazing, formed by clipping to amaze and adding the nonsense suffix -balls (as in cuteballs). It appears online about 2008, was popularized by celebrity bloggers including Perez Hilton, and was famously added to the online Collins English Dictionary in 2012 after a public vote, prompting a round of complaints about the decline of English. By the mid-2010s it was used chiefly ironically.
biblical_def: Amazeballs means "amazing," said with a wink: a word that knows it is a little ridiculous. It belongs to the Millennial habit of playful inflation, where everything good is "amazing" and the extra suffix makes the word funny again. The Christian observation: there is nothing sinful in a silly word, and Christians are allowed to be playful. But the habit behind it, inflating ordinary things into wonders, has a cost, and the root word deserves a second look. In Webster’s 1828, to amaze was "To confound with fear, sudden surprise, or wonder." That is the word the Gospels use for real encounters with God. When Jesus healed the paralytic, "they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion" (Mar 2:12). After the resurrection the women fled the tomb, "for they trembled and were amazed" (Mar 16:8). True amazement is the right response to the works of God, and it is not cheap. A people who spend "amazing" on lip gloss may have nothing left when they stand before the empty tomb. "Marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well" (Psa 139:14). A father can laugh at amazeballs with his teenager, and then take him outside on a clear night, or to the bedside of a newborn, and let him feel what amazement actually is.
webster_summary: Millennial jokey slang (c. 2008; Collins online 2012) for amazing; harmless play, though its root, amaze, names the trembling wonder the Gospels reserve for the works of God (Mar 16:8).
webster_full: AMAZEBALLS, adj. (Millennial slang, c. 2008–2010s; from amaze + jocular -balls) Amazing; excellent; usually said ironically. "Your cupcakes are amazeballs."

Webster (1828), root amaze: AMAZE, verb transitive To confound with fear, sudden surprise, or wonder; to astonish. They shall be afraid; they shall be amazed at one another. Isaiah 23:1 . They were all amazed and glorified God. Mark 2:12 . Luke 5:26 . This word implies astonishment or perplexity, arising from something extraordinary, unexpected, unaccountable, or frightful.
Decode for parents: harmless; a chance to show children what real amazement feels like.
scriptures: Mar 2:12
And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion.
Mar 16:8
And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
Psa 8:1
O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens.
Luk 5:26
And they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day.
corruption_summary: Amazeballs is playful inflation; its only lesson is the cheapening of amazement, which Scripture keeps for the works of God that make men tremble.
corruption_paragraphs: The quiet drift is that wonder becomes a tone of voice rather than a response to reality. When everything is amazing, nothing amazes, and the young lose the experience of being stopped in their tracks. The crowds who saw Jesus heal "were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day" (Luk 5:26). Amazement in Scripture is never a casual adjective; it is a man undone by glory.

The recovery is not to ban silly words but to cultivate real wonder. "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" (Psa 8:1). Read the young the miracles slowly, show them the stars, let them hold a newborn, and talk about what it means. Then their "amazeballs" at a dessert will stay a joke, and their amazement before God will be the real thing.
roots_summary: Old English amasian (to stupefy) → amaze (to confound with fear or wonder) → amazing → c. 2008 amazeballs → Collins online 2012.
roots_lines: Old English amasian — to stun, to confound; compare maze
Webster 1828: amaze — to confound with fear, sudden surprise, or wonder
c. 2008: amazeballs online; popularized by celebrity bloggers
2012: added to Collins online after a public vote
Biblical anchor: they trembled and were amazed (Mar 16:8)
usage: "That concert was amazeballs."
Save true amazement for the works of God (Mar 2:12).
We have seen strange things to day (Luk 5:26).

etymology: A clipped form of whatever, used as a dismissive reply. The dismissive "whatever" itself was a Gen X and 1990s Valley-girl staple (the film Clueless, 1995, made the W-hand gesture famous); Millennials shortened it to whatevs in the 2000s, keeping the shrug but adding a lighter, playful tone. It signals indifference, resignation, or a refusal to argue ("Fine, whatevs").
biblical_def: Whatevs is the verbal shrug: I don’t care, it doesn’t matter, I’m not going to fight about it. Sometimes it is a healthy letting-go of something trivial. Often it is something else: a way of ending a conversation without resolving it, of hiding hurt behind indifference, or of declaring that nothing matters very much. The Christian observation: Scripture asks Christians to care about the right things and to release the wrong ones, and "whatevs" blurs the line. There is a godly whatever. Paul could say of his circumstances, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11), and he told believers to let small offences go. And there is a godly whatever that is the opposite of a shrug: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure … think on these things" (Php 4:8); "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23). The sinful whatevs is lukewarmness. The Lord Jesus said to a church that had shrugged its way into comfort, "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot" (Rev 3:15). A father hears "whatevs" from a teenager and asks, gently, "Does this matter to you or not?" Some things should be released; some things, like faith, family, and right and wrong, deserve a heart that is hot, not a shrug.
webster_summary: Millennial clipped form (2000s) of the dismissive whatever; fine for releasing trifles, dangerous as lukewarm indifference, which Christ rebukes (Rev 3:15) while Paul fills whatsoever with zeal (Php 4:8; Col 3:23).
webster_full: WHATEVS, interj. (Millennial slang, 2000s–2010s; clipped from dismissive whatever) Expresses indifference, resignation, or refusal to argue. "Fine. Whatevs."

Webster (1828), root whatever: WHATEVER, pronoun [what and ever.] 1. Being this or that; being of one nature or another; being one thing or another; any thing that may be. whatever is read, let it be read with attention. whatever measure may be adopted, let it be with due caution. whatever you do, let it be done with prudence. 2. All that; the whole that; all particulars that. At once came forth whatever creeps.
Decode for parents: a "whatevs" about dinner is fine; a "whatevs" about God, honesty, or a friend’s pain needs a conversation.
scriptures: Rev 3:15
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
corruption_summary: Whatevs can release trifles or shrug off what matters; Scripture rebukes lukewarm indifference and fills "whatsoever" with zeal and contentment.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is indifference as a posture. The shrug protects the shrugger from disappointment and conflict, but it also protects him from love, conviction, and effort. A generation that learned to meet everything with "whatever" found it hard to care about anything with its whole heart, including God. Lukewarmness is not a neutral state in Scripture; it is the condition that makes the Lord say He will spue the church out of His mouth.

The recovery is to sort what matters and then to care fully. "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). Christians should be relaxed about the trivial and fervent about the eternal, content in their circumstances and zealous in their callings. Teach the young to let go of small slights without a sulky shrug, and to bring their whole hearts to the things God says are worth caring about.
roots_lines: Old English hwaet + aefre — what + ever
1970s–90s: dismissive "whatever"; 1995 Clueless, the W-hand
2000s: Millennial clipped whatevs
Same family: totes, obvi, probs
Biblical anchor: neither cold nor hot (Rev 3:15); whatsoever ye do, do it heartily (Col 3:23)
usage: "You took the last cookie? Whatevs."
Whatsoever things are true … think on these things (Php 4:8): the godly whatever.
I would thou wert cold or hot (Rev 3:15).

etymology: A playful clipping of jealous, by sound-alike with jelly (the spread). Recorded online from the mid-2000s and spread by reality television (notably Jersey Shore, 2009–2012) and social media, where "jelly" and "so jelly" replaced "jealous" in light, teasing use. Variants: jelly much?, don’t be jelly, and the peanut-butter-and-jelly emoji jokes.
biblical_def: To be jelly is to be jealous, but cutely: "Your vacation pics make me so jelly." The word turns envy into a compliment, a way of saying "I wish I had what you have" with a smile. The Christian observation: the playfulness is often innocent, but the slang works by making a serious sin sound like dessert. Scripture does not treat envy as cute. "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones" (Pro 14:30). "For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work" (Jas 3:16). Envy murdered Abel and sold Joseph; it was "for envy" that the chief priests delivered Jesus to Pilate (Mar 15:10). The word jealous also has a holy sense, and it is worth teaching: "for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God" (Exo 20:5). God’s jealousy is the right zeal of a husband for his wife’s faithfulness; it is love that will not share its beloved with idols. Human envy is the opposite: resentment of another’s good. The cure for envy is contentment and rejoicing: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice" (Rom 12:15). A father hears his daughter say she is "so jelly" of a friend’s new car and asks, half-joking, half-serious, "Are you happy for her?" If the answer is yes, the word is a compliment; if not, it is a sin with a sweet name.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (mid-2000s; Jersey Shore era) for jealous, envious; a cute name for a serious sin, the rottenness of the bones (Pro 14:30), distinct from God’s holy jealousy (Exo 20:5).
webster_full: JELLY, adj. (Millennial slang, mid-2000s–2010s; clipped from jealous) Jealous, envious, usually in teasing or complimentary use. "So jelly of your beach trip." "Jelly much?"

Webster (1828), root jealous: JEALOUS, adjective jel’us. 1. Suspicious; apprehensive of rivalship; uneasy through fear that another has withdrawn or may withdraw from one the affections of a person he loves, or enjoy some good which he desires to obtain; followed by of, and applied both to the object of love and to the rival. We say, a young man is jealous of the woman he loves, or jealous of his rival. A man is jealous of his wife, and the wife of her husband. 2. […]
Decode for parents: ask whether "jelly" means "I’m happy for you" or "I resent you"; the answer decides whether it is a compliment or a sin.
scriptures: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
Jas 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
For he knew that the chief priests had delivered him for envy.
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
corruption_summary: Jelly gives envy a sweet name; Scripture calls envy the rottenness of the bones and contrasts it with God’s holy jealousy and the joy that rejoices with others.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is euphemism. A culture that scrolls through other people’s best moments all day is soaked in envy, and "jelly" makes the feeling acceptable, even fun to admit. But envy is no small sin; it sits in Paul’s list beside murder (Rom 1:29), and it destroys the envier first. Social media is an envy machine, and a cute word lowers the guard just when it most needs raising.

The recovery is contentment and rejoicing. The envious heart resents another’s good; the loving heart is glad of it. Teach the young to notice envy in themselves and name it honestly, to thank God for what He has given them, and to practise congratulating friends sincerely. And teach them the one holy jealousy: God’s fierce, faithful love for His people, which wants their hearts whole.
roots_summary: Greek zēlos (zeal) → Latin zelosus → Old French gelos → jealous → mid-2000s punning clip jelly.
roots_lines: Greek zēlos — zeal, ardour; jealousy
Old French gelos → Middle English jelous
Mid-2000s: jelly by pun on the spread; reality TV spreads it
Phrases: so jelly, jelly much?, don’t be jelly
Biblical anchor: envy the rottenness of the bones (Pro 14:30); I the LORD thy God am a jealous God (Exo 20:5)
usage: "You’re going to Italy? So jelly."
Envy is the rottenness of the bones (Pro 14:30), not a dessert.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice (Rom 12:15).

etymology: A respelling of work as an exclamation of approval for someone performing or looking fierce ("Werk!", "Work it"). It comes from the 1980s New York ballroom scene documented in the film Paris Is Burning (1990), where contestants were cheered to "work" the runway, and it was carried into pop culture by RuPaul’s 1992 hit "Supermodel (You Better Work)" and later by television, especially in the 2010s. Millennials used it as praise for a great outfit, a strong performance, or confidence in general.
biblical_def: "Werk!" is a cheer: you are performing, posing, or presenting yourself with flair, and you are nailing it. The word comes from the runway, where work means strutting with total confidence before an audience. The Christian observation: the cheer itself is light, and encouraging a friend is good. But it is worth noticing what the slang has done to the word work. In Scripture, work is one of the first gifts of God: "the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it" (Gen 2:15), before the fall. Work is service, craftsmanship, and provision. "Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23). The runway werk turns that word inside out: the work is self-display, the audience is men, and the reward is applause. Paul has a sentence for that too: "Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart" (Eph 6:6). The origin of the slang also matters for a Christian parent: it comes from a subculture organized around sexual and gender confusion, which Scripture calls sin, and the word carries some of that world’s values. A father can let his daughter tell her friend "werk" about a great recital, and also teach her that the best work is done for an audience of One, often with no applause at all, and that her worth is not in how well she struts.
webster_summary: Millennial slang from 1980s ballroom culture (Paris Is Burning; RuPaul, 1992) cheering a confident performance; harmless as encouragement, but it turns work from service before God into display before men (Col 3:23; Eph 6:6).
webster_full: WERK, interj. / v. (Millennial slang, 1980s ballroom → 2010s pop; respelling of work) An exclamation praising a confident, stylish performance or look. "Werk!" Also "work it," "you better work."

Webster (1828), root work: WORK, verb intransitive [G., Gr.] 1. In a general sense, to move, or to move one way and the other; to perform; as in popular language it is said, a mill or machine works well. 2. To labor; to be occupied in performing manual labor, whether severe or moderate. One man works better than another; one man works hare; another works lazily. 3. To be in action or motion; as the working of the heart. 4. To act; to carry on operations. Our better part remains to work in close design. 5. To operate; to carry on business; […]
Decode for parents: encourage your children’s performances, and teach them that the deepest work is done for God, unseen.
scriptures: Gen 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Eph 6:6
Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart;
Mat 6:1
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
corruption_summary: Werk turns work from service before God into performance for applause; the cheer is light, but the root word deserves to be restored.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the redefinition of work as display. In the runway world the best "work" is the most commanding self-presentation, and the value of a person is measured by the crowd’s reaction. The Lord Jesus warned against that motive even in religious acts: "Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven" (Mat 6:1). Work done to be seen is already paid in full.

The recovery is the dignity of real labour. "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). The carpenter, the nurse, the mother, the farmer, and the student working quietly for God’s glory are doing the work the slang has forgotten. Cheer your children on in their gifts and performances, and teach them that the highest compliment is not "werk" but "Well done, thou good and faithful servant."
roots_summary: Old English weorc (deed, labour) → work → 1980s ballroom "work the runway" → 1992 RuPaul → 2010s respelling werk.
roots_lines: Old English weorc — deed, action, labour
1980s: New York ballroom culture, "work" = perform with flair; Paris Is Burning (1990)
1992: "Supermodel (You Better Work)"
2010s: television and social media spread werk
Biblical anchor: put him into the garden to dress it and to keep it (Gen 2:15); do it heartily, as to the Lord (Col 3:23)
usage: "New haircut? Werk!"
Work as to the Lord, and not unto men (Col 3:23).
The best compliment: Well done, thou good and faithful servant.

etymology: An emphatic, drawn-out yes, often "yaaas," used to cheer someone or something. Like werk, it circulated in 1980s–90s ballroom culture, and it reached the mainstream through the comedy series Broad City (2014), whose "Yas, queen!" became a catchphrase, then a meme, then a cliché. By 2016 it was used for any enthusiastic approval ("yas to tacos").
biblical_def: Yas is yes with the volume turned up: enthusiastic, celebratory approval. "Yas, queen!" cheers a friend; "yaaas" greets a favourite song. The Christian observation: the word is mostly harmless, a loud yes of delight, and delight is a good thing. Scripture is full of enthusiastic yeses. The people answered Ezra’s blessing, "Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands" (Neh 8:6). The best yes in the Bible is God’s own: "For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us" (2Co 1:20). In Christ, God says yes to every promise He has made. That gives a Christian a reason for a much bigger yas than a new pair of boots. There are two cautions. First, the hype culture around "yas, queen" can make approval automatic: every choice gets cheered, whether wise or foolish, and friends stop telling each other the truth. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" (Pro 27:6). Second, a Christian’s yes should mean yes: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay" (Jas 5:12). A loud yes to everything is a quiet way of meaning nothing. A father enjoys his children’s enthusiasm, and he teaches them to save their loudest yes for what God says yes to, and to be the kind of friend whose yas means something because it is not automatic.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (ballroom culture; Broad City, 2014) for an emphatic, celebratory yes; harmless delight, best when it echoes God’s great yes in Christ (2Co 1:20) and does not become automatic hype.
webster_full: YAS, interj. (Millennial slang, 2014–present; emphatic yes; also yaas, yaaas) Enthusiastic approval or excitement. "Yas, queen!" "Yas to Friday."
Webster (1828), root yes: YES, adverb A word which expresses affirmation or consent; opposed to no; […]
Decode for parents: enjoy the enthusiasm; teach your children to be friends whose yes is not automatic.
scriptures: For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.
Neh 8:6
And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God. And all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands: and they bowed their heads, and worshipped the LORD with their faces to the ground.
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
corruption_summary: Yas is happy enthusiasm; its only drift is automatic hype that cheers every choice, while Scripture’s greatest yes is God’s in Christ and a believer’s yes should mean yes.
corruption_paragraphs: The small corruption is cheerleading without judgment. "Yas, queen" culture cheers every outfit, decision, and declaration, and in its strongest forms it treats any hesitation as betrayal. Friends who only say yas cannot help each other; they can only applaud. "Open rebuke is better than secret love" (Pro 27:5), and a friend who never says "wait" is not much of a friend.

The redemption is joy with discernment. "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it" (Psa 118:24): Christians have every reason for loud, delighted yeses. Teach the young to cheer each other wholeheartedly for what is good, to speak honestly when a friend is heading the wrong way, and to sing their loudest amen to the promises of God that are all yea in Christ.
roots_summary: Old English gise (so be it) → yes → ballroom emphatic yas → 2014 Broad City "Yas, queen!" → 2016 meme and cliché.

usage: "Snow day tomorrow?! Yaaas!"
God’s great yas: all the promises of God in him are yea (2Co 1:20).
Let your yea be yea (Jas 5:12).

etymology: From receipt, a written acknowledgment of something received, and so proof of a transaction. In 2010s Black Twitter and then general social media, receipts meant evidence, typically screenshots of texts, posts, or messages, used to prove a claim or expose a lie ("I have the receipts"; "show receipts"). The phrase got wider attention around 2014–2016 in celebrity feuds where screenshots were posted to settle disputes. The Oxford English Dictionary notes the slang sense.
biblical_def: Receipts, in social-media slang, are proof: the screenshots of a conversation, the saved post, the timestamped message that shows who said what. "She says she never said it? I have receipts." The Christian observation: the demand for evidence is deeply biblical, and so is the warning about how evidence is used. Scripture refused to convict anyone on a single unsupported accusation: "at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established" (Deu 19:15). Paul repeats it for church discipline (2Co 13:1). So "show receipts" is, in a sense, an ancient principle. The danger is in what screenshot culture does with receipts. It keeps files on friends, saves private words to use later, and releases them publicly to humiliate. That is not justice but exposure, and Scripture forbids it. Jesus gave a process for a brother’s sin: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone" (Mat 18:15), not between thee and the whole internet. Love "thinketh no evil" (1Co 13:5); it does not keep a ledger of another’s worst words. "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends" (Pro 17:9). A father teaches his children: never accuse without proof, never assume guilt without hearing both sides (Pro 18:17), and never save a friend’s private words as ammunition. Bring evidence to the right people, privately and humbly, for restoration, not for a crowd.
webster_summary: Millennial social-media slang (2010s) for evidence, especially screenshots that prove a claim; biblical in demanding proof (Deu 19:15), sinful when kept as ammunition and published to expose rather than restore (Mat 18:15; Pro 17:9).
webster_full: RECEIPTS, n. pl. (Millennial social-media slang, 2010s–present; from receipt, proof of a transaction) Evidence, especially screenshots of messages or posts, used to prove a claim or expose a lie. "Show receipts." "I’ve got the receipts."

Webster (1828), root receipt: RECEIPT, RECE’IT, noun rece’t. [Latin receptus. This word wought to follow the analogy of conceit, deceit, from Latin conceptus, deceptus, and be written without p, receit.] 1. The act of receiving; as the receit of a letter. 2. The place of receiving; as the receit of custom. Matthew 9:9 . 3. Reception; as the receit of blessings or mercies. 4. Reception; welcome; as the kind receit of a friend. obsolete [In this sense, reception is now used.] 5. Recipe; […]
Decode for parents: ask whether your child keeps screenshots of friends’ messages, and why.
scriptures: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
Pro 17:9
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
corruption_summary: Receipts rightly demands proof, but screenshot culture keeps files on friends and publishes them to humiliate; Scripture requires evidence and forbids exposure without love.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is evidence weaponized. Screenshot culture trains young people to treat every private conversation as a potential exhibit, to keep receipts on friends, and to "drop" them when a relationship sours. Trust collapses when every word might be published; friends become prosecutors. Proverbs names the cost: he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends. And the public receipt-drop skips every step of the Lord’s process for dealing with sin.

The recovery holds both halves. Evidence matters: do not believe or spread an accusation without proof, and remember that "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Pro 18:17). Love matters more: deal with a brother’s fault privately first, aim at restoration, and never hoard someone’s worst moment. Teach the young to be fair-minded witnesses and faithful friends, and to delete what they were only keeping to hurt someone.
roots_summary: Latin recipere (to receive) → receipt (acknowledgment of what is received; proof) → 2010s social-media receipts (screenshot evidence).
roots_lines: Latin recipere — to take back, to receive; recepta — things received
Middle English receite — a receiving; then a written acknowledgment
2010s: Black Twitter receipts — proof, screenshots
2014–2016: celebrity feuds settled by posted screenshots
Biblical anchor: at the mouth of two witnesses (Deu 19:15); tell him his fault between thee and him alone (Mat 18:15)
usage: "He swears he didn’t text her? She’s got receipts."
Require proof (Deu 19:15); then go to him alone (Mat 18:15).
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love (Pro 17:9).

etymology: From Latin extra (outside, beyond), long used in English as an adjective for "additional." The slang sense, excessive, over the top, dramatic, trying too hard, comes from African-American usage and became widespread in the mid-2010s on Twitter and Instagram ("she’s so extra"). It describes both behaviour (a dramatic reaction) and style (an elaborate outfit), and it can be mildly critical or affectionate. Gen Z continued it, sometimes approvingly.
biblical_def: To be extra is to be too much: the dramatic reaction, the over-planned birthday, the outfit with three more accessories than necessary, the person who turns everything into a production. It can be an affectionate tease or a real criticism. The Christian observation: Scripture actually has a word for the opposite of extra, and it is a virtue. "Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand" (Php 4:5). The old word moderation means gentleness, reasonableness, a life that is not always pressing to the edge. Proverbs warns against the person who must always be seen and heard: "A fool’s mouth is his destruction" (Pro 18:7), and "Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it" (Pro 25:16). And the Lord Jesus warned against religious extraness: the hypocrites who "love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men" (Mat 6:5). There is a holy extra, though. The woman who broke an alabaster box of very precious ointment over Jesus’ head was called extra by the disciples ("To what purpose is this waste?"), and Jesus defended her: "she hath wrought a good work upon me" (Mat 26:10). Lavish love for Christ is never too much. A father tells his children: be moderate in everything that is about you, and extravagant in everything that is about Him.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (mid-2010s, from AAVE) for excessive, dramatic, over the top; Scripture prizes moderation (Php 4:5) and rebukes display (Mat 6:5), yet defends the lavish extravagance of love for Christ (Mat 26:10).
webster_full: EXTRA, adj. (Millennial slang, mid-2010s–present; AAVE origin) Excessive; over the top; dramatic; trying too hard. "He’s so extra." Used of behaviour, style, or celebrations.
Webster (1828), root extra: EXTRA, A Latin preposition, denoting beyond or excess; as extra-work, extra-pay, work or pay beyond what is usual or agreed on.
Decode for parents: when a child is "extra," ask whether the extra is about himself or about someone he loves.
scriptures: Php 4:5
Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand.
Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it.
Mat 6:5

And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
When Jesus understood it, he said unto them, Why trouble ye the woman? for she hath wrought a good work upon me.
Mat 26:8
But when his disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose is this waste?
corruption_summary: Extra names excess and self-display; Scripture prizes moderation in what concerns the self and defends extravagance only in love for Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption in being extra is usually self-focus. The over-the-top reaction makes the moment about the reactor; the elaborate production makes the event about the producer. Social media rewards it, because extra gets noticed. But the Lord’s warning about prayer "to be seen of men" applies to every kind of performance: those who do things to be seen "have their reward," and it is a thin one.

The redemption is to aim the extravagance rightly. When the disciples complained, "To what purpose is this waste?" (Mat 26:8), they thought the woman was extra; Jesus said her act would be told wherever the gospel is preached. Teach the young that moderation in food, speech, dress, and drama is a mark of maturity, and that lavish worship, generous giving, and costly love for Christ are never too much.
roots_summary: Latin extra (outside, beyond) → English adjective extra (additional) → AAVE / mid-2010s social media extra (over the top).
roots_lines: Latin extra — outside, beyond, besides
17th–18th c.: English extra — additional, beyond the usual
Mid-2010s: AAVE and Twitter extra — excessive, dramatic
Gen Z continues it, sometimes as praise
Biblical anchor: let your moderation be known unto all men (Php 4:5); she hath wrought a good work upon me (Mat 26:10)
usage: "A fog machine for a ninth birthday? So extra."
Let your moderation be known unto all men (Php 4:5).
The alabaster box was not extra; it was love (Mat 26:10).

etymology: From Old French sauvage, Latin silvaticus (of the woods, wild). In mid-2010s slang, especially from about 2015 on Twitter, Instagram, and in hip-hop (21 Savage; Megan Thee Stallion’s "Savage," 2020), savage became praise for someone who is brutally honest, fearless, or cuttingly witty, or for a comeback or "roast" so harsh it is admired ("that reply was savage"). It also describes someone indifferent to others’ feelings, as a compliment.
biblical_def: In Millennial and Gen Z slang, to be savage is to be ruthlessly bold: the comeback that humiliates, the breakup text with no mercy, the person who says exactly what everyone was thinking and does not care who bleeds. "That roast was savage" is high praise. The Christian observation: the slang admires something Scripture calls sin. Cruelty is not courage. "The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh" (Pro 11:17). "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6): salt, yes, but grace first. The tongue that cuts for sport is the one James calls "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8). The savage persona is often admired because it seems free, unbothered by approval, and that freedom is worth having; Christians should not be people-pleasers. But Scripture gives a different source for it: the man who fears God fears no one else, and so he can tell the truth gently. "Speaking the truth in love" (Eph 4:15) takes more courage than a savage roast, because it costs the speaker something. Paul tells believers to put off "anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth" (Col 3:8). A father tells his son: be brave enough to tell the truth to anyone, and kind enough that the truth can be received. The world calls cruelty savage; the Bible calls meekness strength.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (mid-2010s) praising brutal, cutting boldness or a merciless roast; it admires cruelty as courage, which Scripture rejects for truth spoken in love (Pro 11:17; Eph 4:15). Reject.
webster_full: SAVAGE, adj. / n. (Millennial and Gen Z slang, c. 2015–present) Brutally bold; ruthlessly honest or cutting, used as praise. "That comeback was savage." As a noun: a person who acts this way.

Webster (1828), root savage: SAVAGE, adjective [Latin silva, a wood, or silvicola, an inhabitant of a wood, or silvaticus.] 1. Pertaining to the forest; wild; remote from human residence and improvements; uncultivated; as a savage wilderness. Cornels and savage berries of the wood. 2. Wild; untamed; as savage beasts of prey. 3. Uncivilized; untaught; unpolished; rude; as savage life; savage manners. What nation since the commencement of the christian era, ever rose from savage to civilized without christianity? 4. Cruel; barbarous; fierce; ferocious; […]
Decode for parents: when your child praises a "savage" reply, ask how the person on the other end felt.
scriptures: The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
Jas 3:8
But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
Eph 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
Col 3:8
But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth.
corruption_summary: Savage praises cruelty as courage and cutting speech as freedom; Scripture names cruelty sin and demands the harder courage of truth spoken in love.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the moral inversion in the compliment. A word that once meant uncivilized and cruel became a badge of honour, and the young learned that the highest social achievement is to wound someone cleverly in public. The "savage" reply gets likes; the gentle answer gets ignored. Over time that reward system forms people who are quick to cut and slow to heal.

The recovery is meekness, which is strength under control, not weakness. "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Pro 15:1), and it takes far more self-mastery than a roast. Teach the young to admire the courage of the truth-teller who risks something for another’s good, to refuse the applause for cruelty, and to notice that the Lord Jesus, who could have silenced every enemy with a word, answered them with truth and died for them.
roots_summary: Latin silva (forest) → silvaticus (wild) → Old French sauvage → English savage (wild, cruel) → c. 2015 slang praise for brutal boldness.

Old French sauvage → Middle English savage — wild, fierce, cruel
c. 2015: social-media and hip-hop savage — ruthless, admired
2020: "Savage" (Megan Thee Stallion) cements the sense
Biblical anchor: he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh (Pro 11:17); speaking the truth in love (Eph 4:15)
usage: "She told him off in front of everyone. Savage."
A soft answer turneth away wrath (Pro 15:1): that is strength.
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).

etymology: From the slang verb to hook up (to meet, to connect; by the 1980s–90s, deliberately vague slang for any sexual encounter from kissing to intercourse). The phrase hookup culture appeared in campus journalism and sociology in the late 1990s and 2000s (Kathleen Bogle’s Hooking Up, 2008; Donna Freitas’s The End of Sex, 2013) to describe the norm, especially on college campuses, of casual sexual encounters without relationship or commitment. Dating apps in the 2010s extended it beyond campuses.
biblical_def: Hookup culture is the social norm that casual sexual encounters, without love, commitment, or even a second meeting, are an ordinary part of young adult life. The vagueness of "hooking up" is part of the design: it can mean anything, so it commits to nothing. The Christian observation must be clear, because the culture is not. Scripture places sex inside the covenant of marriage and nowhere else: "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge" (Heb 13:4). It names sex outside marriage fornication and gives a plain command: "Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body" (1Co 6:18). Paul explains why casual sex is impossible in God’s design: "What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh" (1Co 6:16). There is no such thing as a meaningless hookup; the body makes a covenant gesture the heart is refusing. The culture promised freedom and delivered loneliness, regret, and wounded souls, and the researchers who studied it found that many students quietly wanted something else. The gospel offers that something else, and it offers it to those already wounded: "Such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified" (1Co 6:11). A father tells his son and daughter, plainly and early: your body is not a toy, sex is a covenant gift, and the person worth giving it to will wait for vows. And if you have already fallen, Christ washes.
webster_summary: Millennial-era term (late 1990s–2010s campus sociology; dating apps) for the norm of casual, uncommitted sexual encounters; Scripture calls it fornication, places sex within marriage (Heb 13:4), and offers washing to the fallen (1Co 6:11). Reject.
webster_full: HOOKUP CULTURE, n. (Millennial-era sociological and campus slang, late 1990s–present) A social norm accepting casual sexual encounters without relationship or commitment. To hook up: deliberately vague slang for any sexual encounter.

Webster (1828), root hook: HOOK, noun 1. A piece of iron or other metal bent into a curve for catching, holding and sustaining any thing; as a hook for catching fish; a teeter-hook; a chimney-hook; a pot-hook, etc. 2. A snare; a trap. 3. A curving instrument for cutting grass or grain; a sickle; an instrument for cutting or lopping. 4. That part of a hinge which is fixed or inserted in a post. Whence the phrase, to be off the hooks, to be unhinged, to be disturbed or disordered. 5. A forked timber in a ship, placed on the keel. 6. A catch; […]
Decode for parents: "hook up" is vague on purpose; ask your teenager what it means in their circle, and tell them plainly what God says.
scriptures: Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.
What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh.
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
corruption_summary: Hookup culture makes uncommitted sex normal and calls it freedom; Scripture names it fornication, explains why no union of bodies is casual, and offers cleansing in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the separation of the body from the covenant. Hookup culture treats sex as recreation, detachable from love, promise, and children, and it builds a social world where restraint looks strange and commitment looks naive. But the body does not obey the theory. Paul’s argument is that sexual union always makes "one flesh"; it is a covenant act whether or not the people intend one. The result is a generation that has given itself away piecemeal and finds it hard to give itself wholly to anyone.

The recovery is both a standard and a mercy. The standard: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour" (1Th 4:3-4). The mercy: the Corinthian church was full of people who had lived the hookup life of their pagan city, and Paul did not say they were ruined; he said they were washed. Teach the young the plain truth before the culture teaches them a lie, and make sure every one of them knows that Christ cleanses the fallen and restores the wounded.
roots_summary: Old English hoc (hook) → to hook up (to connect) → 1980s–90s vague sexual slang → late 1990s–2000s hookup culture → 2010s dating apps.

20th c.: hook up — to connect, to meet
1980s–90s: hook up as deliberately vague sexual slang
2000s: hookup culture in campus sociology (Bogle, 2008; Freitas, 2013); 2010s dating apps
Biblical anchor: marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled (Heb 13:4); flee fornication (1Co 6:18)
usage: "Nobody dates here; it’s all hookup culture."
There is no casual union: two shall be one flesh (1Co 6:16).
Such were some of you: but ye are washed (1Co 6:11).
